## Introduction

In economics, we are very used to the idea of distinguishing between the treatment and other variables that we want to *control for*.  To fix ideas, suppose we are interested in the effect of a binary treatment variable, $$D$$, and want to control for a vector of covariates $$X$$.

When we say that we want to control for certain variables, we mean that we would like to compare outcomes for units that are the same in terms of those variables, while being different in terms of the treatment variable.  In other words, we want to report an average of the *conditional contrasts*

$$\delta(x) := m_1(x) - m_0(x) = \E[Y \mid X=x, D=1] - \E[Y \mid X=x, D=0]$$

Many approaches to causal inference are based on making exactly this kind of comparison, including matching [@heckman-ichimura-todd-1997], regression adjustment (where one estimates $$m_0(x)$$ and uses it to impute untreated potential outcomes for treated units), and (at least to some extent) regressions of the outcome on the treatment and covariates.  And I think it is the most natural way to think about what role we want covariates to play in empirical applications.

Moreover, under the following unconfoundedness assumption

$$Y(0) \independent D \mid X$$

it follows that

$$\delta(x) = \ATT(x)$$

One more thing that is often under-emphasized in economics is that, for $$\delta(x)$$ to be well defined, there need to be both treated and untreated units with covariates $$x$$.  That is, we need *overlap*, $$0 < p(x) < 1$$.  Without it, it's infeasible to compare treated and untreated units with the same covariates.

### Covariate Balancing

The other paradigm for using covariates in empirical work is based on *balancing*.  Balancing is less common in economics, and, for me, a bit harder to think about.

Rather than explicitly making comparisons within values of $$X$$, the idea is to reweight the groups so that they have the same distribution of covariates and then compare (weighted) mean outcomes.  This is the language of the propensity score reweighting literature [@hirano-imbens-ridder-2003], as well as of methods like entropy balancing [@hainmueller-2012] and the covariate balancing propensity score [@imai-ratkovic-2014].

### Connecting Controlling and Balancing

It's not immediately clear what "controlling" and "balancing" have to do with each other.  We will explore this below.  I'll start with the case where the target parameter is the $$\ATT$$ and then generalize.

## Case 1: ATT

Suppose that we are interested in the average treatment effect on the treated, $$\ATT := \E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid D=1]$$.  By the law of iterated expectations and unconfoundedness, it immediately follows that

$$\ATT = \E[\ATT(X) \mid D=1] = \E[\delta(X) \mid D=1]$$

In other words, the $$\ATT$$ is the average of the conditional contrasts over the distribution of covariates for the treated group.

### Controlling is Balancing

Famously, the $$\ATT$$ can also be written in terms of propensity score weights [@rosenbaum-rubin-1983; @imbens-wooldridge-2009].  To see this, split $$\E[\delta(X) \mid D=1]$$ into two terms,

$$\E[\delta(X) \mid D=1] = \E[Y \mid D=1] - \E[m_0(X) \mid D=1]$$

and then change the distribution that the second term averages over,

$$\begin{aligned}
\E[m_0(X) \mid D=1] &= \E[w_0(X) m_0(X) \mid D=0] \\
&= \E[w_0(X) Y \mid D=0]
\end{aligned}$$

where

$$w_0(x) := \frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)} = \frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)} \frac{1-\pi}{\pi}$$

The first equality reweights the untreated group's distribution of covariates to match the treated group's (the second expression for the weights comes from Bayes' rule).  The second equality uses the law of iterated expectations, which works here because the weights only depend on $$X$$.  Putting these together,

$$\ATT = \E[Y \mid D=1] - \E[w_0(X) Y \mid D=0]$$

A key property of the weights $$w_0(x)$$ is that they balance the distribution of covariates.  For any function $$g$$,

$$\E[w_0(X) g(X) \mid D=0] = \E[g(X) \mid D=1]$$

so that, after reweighting, the untreated group has the same distribution of covariates as the treated group.

This is the sense in which controlling is balancing.  Targeting the $$\ATT$$ by controlling for $$X$$ is *the same* as reweighting the untreated group so that its distribution of covariates matches the treated group and then comparing means.

### Balancing is Controlling

Now let's go in the other direction.  Suppose that we have some weights $$\tilde{w}_0(X)$$ for the untreated group that balance the distribution of covariates, so that

$$\E[\tilde{w}_0(X) g(X) \mid D=0] = \E[g(X) \mid D=1] \quad \text{for all functions } g$$

Then the difference between the mean outcome for the treated group and the weighted mean outcome for the untreated group is

$$\begin{aligned}
\E[Y \mid D=1] - \E[\tilde{w}_0(X) Y \mid D=0] &= \E[Y \mid D=1] - \E[\tilde{w}_0(X) m_0(X) \mid D=0] \\
&= \E[Y \mid D=1] - \E[m_0(X) \mid D=1] \\
&= \E[\delta(X) \mid D=1] \\
&= \ATT
\end{aligned}$$

where the first equality holds by the law of iterated expectations, the second holds by the balancing property (with $$g = m_0$$), the third holds by the definition of $$\delta(x)$$, and the last holds by unconfoundedness.

Thus, balancing delivers exactly the "controlling for" expression from above.^[Strictly speaking, this direction already follows from the previous one.  Taking $$g$$ to be indicator functions in the balancing condition implies that $$\tilde{w}_0(x) f_0(x) = f_1(x)$$, so the only weights that balance the entire distribution of covariates are the propensity score weights $$w_0(x)$$.  The direct argument is still useful, though, because it only uses the balancing property and not the particular form of the weights, and that is the argument that generalizes below.]  In other words, if we can balance the distribution of the covariates to be the same for the untreated group as it is for the treated group, then we can recover the $$\ATT$$ without ever explicitly controlling for $$X$$.

## Case 2: More General Target Parameters

The results above are all well known, and they are what rationalize balancing approaches like propensity score reweighting.  But they do not say much about the estimators that are most common in economics, in particular regressions like

$$Y_i = \alpha D_i + X_i'\beta + e_i$$

Except in special cases, $$\alpha$$ is not the $$\ATT$$.  However, under some conditions and allowing for treatment effect heterogeneity, $$\alpha$$ is a weighted average of the $$\delta(x)$$'s with weights that differ from the ones that deliver the $$\ATT$$.  For example, when the covariates are discrete and the regression is saturated in them, $$\alpha = \E[\omega(X) \delta(X)]$$ with $$\omega(x) \propto p(x)(1-p(x))$$ [@angrist-1998].

Thus, the questions for this section are whether controlling is still balancing, and whether balancing still delivers a "controlling for" parameter.

Along these lines, consider any target parameter of the form

$$\theta_\omega := \E[\omega(X) \delta(X)]$$

where $$\omega(x) \geq 0$$ and $$\E[\omega(X)] = 1$$.  $$\theta_\omega$$ is harder to interpret than the $$\ATT$$, but it still has some merit as a causal parameter because it is a weighted average of the conditional contrasts $$\delta(x)$$.  In other words, it is a weighted average where we "control for" $$X$$.

### Controlling is Balancing

Following the same steps as for the $$\ATT$$, we can write $$\theta_\omega$$ as a difference in weighted means,

$$\theta_\omega = \E[w_1(X) Y \mid D=1] - \E[w_0(X) Y \mid D=0]$$

where

$$w_1(x) := \omega(x) \frac{\pi}{p(x)} \quad \text{and} \quad w_0(x) := \omega(x) \frac{1-\pi}{1-p(x)}$$

which are well defined because of overlap.  These weights have three properties.

1. They are non-negative.

2. They have mean one within each group, $$\E[w_1(X) \mid D=1] = \E[w_0(X) \mid D=0] = 1$$.

3. They balance the two groups to a common distribution of covariates.  For any function $$g$$,

   $$\E[w_1(X) g(X) \mid D=1] = \E[\omega(X) g(X)] = \E[w_0(X) g(X) \mid D=0]$$

The third property says that, even if we are willing to settle for a parameter like $$\theta_\omega$$, controlling for $$X$$ still amounts to balancing the covariates.  After reweighting, both groups have the distribution of covariates whose density is $$\omega(x) f(x)$$.^[Relative to the $$\ATT$$, the difference is that both groups are balanced to the distribution of covariates with density $$\omega(x) f(x)$$ (the population distribution of covariates reweighted by $$\omega$$) rather than to the distribution of covariates for the treated group.  For the $$\ATT$$, $$\omega(x) = p(x)/\pi$$, so $$\omega(x) f(x) = f_1(x)$$ and $$w_1(x) = 1$$, which is why only the untreated group needed to be reweighted.  For the saturated regression above, the target distribution has density proportional to $$p(x)(1-p(x)) f(x)$$, which puts the most weight on values of the covariates where treated and untreated units are both common.]

### Balancing is Controlling

Conversely, consider any weights $$w_1(X)$$ and $$w_0(X)$$ that are non-negative, have mean one in the treated group, and balance the two groups to some common distribution of covariates,

$$\E[w_1(X) g(X) \mid D=1] = \E[w_0(X) g(X) \mid D=0] \quad \text{for all functions } g$$

Then,

$$\begin{aligned}
& \E[w_1(X) Y \mid D=1] - \E[w_0(X) Y \mid D=0] \\
& \quad = \E[w_1(X) m_1(X) \mid D=1] - \E[w_0(X) m_0(X) \mid D=0] \\
& \quad = \E[w_1(X) m_1(X) \mid D=1] - \E[w_1(X) m_0(X) \mid D=1] \\
& \quad = \E[w_1(X) \delta(X) \mid D=1]
\end{aligned}$$

where the second equality uses the balancing property with $$g = m_0$$.  Since the weights are non-negative and have mean one, this is a weighted average of the conditional contrasts.  In fact, it is exactly $$\theta_\omega$$ with $$\omega(x) = w_1(x) p(x) / \pi$$.

This shows that, just as for the $$\ATT$$, when we compare weighted means of the treated and untreated groups, balancing the covariates (to any common distribution) implies that we are implicitly controlling for $$X$$.

### Does "Not Balancing" Imply "Not Controlling"?

The final question is whether a set of weights that does not balance the distribution of covariates could still be "controlling for" $$X$$.

The answer is no.  Consider any weights $$w_1(X)$$ and $$w_0(X)$$.  By the law of iterated expectations,

$$\begin{aligned}
& \E[w_1(X) Y \mid D=1] - \E[w_0(X) Y \mid D=0] \\
& \quad = \E[w_1(X) m_1(X) \mid D=1] - \E[w_0(X) m_0(X) \mid D=0]
\end{aligned}$$

For this to be a "controlling for" parameter, it needs to be equal to $$\theta_\omega$$ for some $$\omega$$, and it needs to be equal to it whatever $$m_1(x)$$ and $$m_0(x)$$ happen to be (unconfoundedness does not restrict them).  Since this has to hold for every $$m_1$$ and $$m_0$$, it has to hold separately for the treated and untreated terms, so that

$$\E[w_1(X) m_1(X) \mid D=1] = \E[\omega(X) m_1(X)] \quad \text{for all functions } m_1$$

and

$$\E[w_0(X) m_0(X) \mid D=0] = \E[\omega(X) m_0(X)] \quad \text{for all functions } m_0$$

The first condition says that reweighting the treated group by $$w_1$$ gives it the distribution of covariates with density $$\omega(x) f(x)$$, and the second condition says the same thing for the untreated group reweighted by $$w_0$$.  Together, they say that

$$\E[w_1(X) g(X) \mid D=1] = \E[w_0(X) g(X) \mid D=0] \quad \text{for all functions } g$$

which is exactly the balancing condition.

In other words, without balance there is no "controlling for".^[This does not mean that an estimator that does not balance the covariates can never give the right answer.  A regression could still work in a particular application, for example if $$m_0(x)$$ is linear in $$x$$ and treatment effects do not vary across $$x$$.  But it would get there by extrapolation, which is not the notion of "controlling for" that we started with.  It is not doing the thing that we wanted it to do originally, and instead relies on functional form assumptions that are generally not the type of assumptions that we want to make.]

## Implications

The discussion above shows the equivalence between controlling for and balancing covariates.  This is interesting to me, but I think there are also some important implications, and it is related to some of my ongoing research.

For many estimators that involve modeling the outcome (e.g., a regression), it is possible to reformulate them as a weighting estimator.  The discussion above highlights that we could potentially assess how well they control for covariates by exploring how well they balance covariates.  There are several papers that do this in the cross-sectional setting [e.g., @chattopadhyay-zubizarreta-2023], and I will explore this in my next post.  This is also exactly the type of approach that we take in @caetano-callaway-2026, where we consider how well different estimators for difference-in-differences (TWFE regressions, @callaway-santanna-2021, and imputation estimators as in @borusyak-jaravel-spiess-2024) control for time-varying covariates by assessing how well they balance the covariates.
